description: Thirty authored retrieval cases grounded in the eight archived ARC topics. Expected targets are fixed before changing ranking. Archived source text and embeddings are not committed.

cases.query: Where did I confuse the value of twice a number with evaluating two conditions at the same input?
I could check the forward implication but kept mixing up which condition was necessary and which was sufficient.
When I negate a strict inequality, why must I include the equality boundary?
My decimal counterexample showed squaring can make a positive number smaller than itself.
Why was the square inequality true for integers but false for real numbers?
I rejected an existential because only one value worked in the finite domain.
Why do successive percentage changes multiply instead of simply adding the percentages?
Multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses its direction.
Principal square root versus both solutions of a square equation.
Absolute value means distance from zero, so absolute value equations can have two branches.
A symmetric secant gave zero at the absolute value corner, but the two one-sided rates disagreed.
The skeptic chooses the error tolerance and I choose a nonzero interval small enough to satisfy it.
I used the total output instead of change in output when computing a finite rate.
How did I control all nearby endpoint pairs using the error bound 6d plus 3d squared?
I treated an upper bound as an equality and assumed two independent offsets had to be equal.
Which vanishing intervals ARC still owed an operational application and unfamiliar transfer after the central proof?
Find the reciprocal function tangent line at two with slope minus one quarter and error small relative to displacement.
Why is a tiny absolute residual insufficient to establish local linearity without dividing by displacement?
Why did the piecewise radical transfer force two incompatible one-sided slopes after the reciprocal local line proof?
How did the binomial expansion prove the general power rule from first principles?
In the power rule work, I confused scaling the output by a constant with scaling the input.
How did real powers and absolute value behavior at zero depend on the exponent convention?
cases.labelCorrection: Source audit found real-power domain conventions in Domain-Safe Algebra; A04 proves positive-integer powers only. Corrected without changing the query or tuning the ranker.

cases.query: Canceling the factor x minus three simplifies the formula but does not restore the excluded input.
Replacing log of x to the negative two by minus two log x loses the negative inputs.
The domain of a real rational power depends on the parity of the reduced denominator.
Squaring the equation square root of x plus six equals x created an extraneous negative candidate.
Dividing by a factor that might be zero can delete a genuine solution branch.
Solve a rational inequality by separating numerator and denominator signs and keeping the forbidden denominator out.
The recovery equation was square root of x divided by x minus two equals one, with candidates one and four.
I kept reversing the restriction on y when choosing reciprocal counterexamples to x squared greater than or equal to x.
